hook: Python syntax will feel **weird for exactly one day** — then it clicks. Five ideas, one reel.

scenes.title: No type declarations. **Ever.**
scenes.sub: The variable is just a name tag on an object

actors.t: wrong type? found at run time

steps.at: In C sharp, you declare the type
In Python, you just name the value

scenes.narration: In C sharp, you declare the type, then the name. In Python, you just name the value. The name is a sticker on the object — peel it off, stick it on something else, even a different type. Python doesn't care. The trade-off: less ceremony, but type errors show up at run time instead of compile time. That's why we'll add type hints later — reel eight.

Side by side: in C sharp, int count equals five locks the sticker to integers. In Python, count equals five just sticks the name on a five. Later, count equals some text is perfectly legal. Nothing is declared; everything is an object with a type of its own. The variable is untyped — the value isn't.

scenes.title: Whitespace **is** the syntax
scenes.sub: Indentation = braces. There is no other way.
scenes.narration: Here's the biggest culture shock: Python has no curly braces. The indentation is the block. If a line is inside an if, it's indented four spaces — that's the whole rule. It's not a style choice like in C sharp; it's the language. The good news: every Python file on Earth looks the same. The bad news: one mixed tab and your day is gone.

Three rules. Four spaces per level — set your editor to convert tabs. A block ends when the indentation ends — unindenting is your closing brace. And everything inside a block must be indented, even a single line. The compiler won't guess your intent — it reads the whitespace, literally.

scenes.title: String interpolation, **upgraded**
scenes.sub: The f-string makes C# interpolation look basic

steps.at: Put an f before a string

do:
# Many formats, one syntax
f"{price:.2f}"
f"{rows:,}"
f"{name=}  # debug"

scenes.narration: Now the fun part. Put an f before a string, and any expression in curly braces is evaluated inside it. But here's what C sharp can't do: format specifiers live right in the braces — colon point two f for floats, colon comma for thousands, even date formatting and alignment. It's the string interpolation you know, with the format string built in.

Look at the power here. f-quote total colon point two f — gives you two decimals. f-quote n colon comma — inserts thousands separators. And the braces take any expression: function calls, math, whatever. One line, no string dot format, no concatenation. You'll use this constantly in logging and LLM prompt building.

scenes.title: null is gone. Meet **None**
scenes.sub: And almost everything can be truthy or falsy

steps.at: nearly every object is either truthy or falsy
Empty string, empty list, zero, None

scenes.narration: C sharp's null becomes None in Python — capital N. Same idea: the absence of a value. But Python goes further: nearly every object is either truthy or falsy. Empty string, empty list, zero, None — all falsy. Non-empty collections and non-zero numbers are truthy. So you can write 'if items:' instead of 'if items dot count greater than zero'.

The falsy family: None, zero, empty string, empty list, empty dict — all read as false. Everything else is true. And one habit from your spec: check for None with 'is None', not double-equals. Is compares identity — is it literally the None object. It's the idiomatic, slightly faster check.

scenes.title: The operators that **surprise** C# devs
scenes.narration: Three operators to rewire in your head. First: double-equals checks value equality, while 'is' checks identity — same object in memory. Second: 'in' tests membership — is this value inside that collection. Third: range generates numbers lazily — range of five is not a list, it's a sequence you iterate once.

steps.at: range of five feeds a loop
If you need an actual list

scenes.narration: In practice: compare data with double-equals, use 'is' only for None and sentinel objects. Membership with 'in' — quote prompt in text — is how you'll check if an LLM's output contains a marker. And range of five feeds a loop zero through four. If you need an actual list, wrap it: list of range five.

scenes.title: Data structures — Python's superpower
scenes.next: Reel 3 · Core Data Structures — list, dict, set, comprehensions

recap: Variables are name tags — untyped, movable, runtime-checked
Indentation IS the block structure — 4 spaces, no braces
f-strings interpolate anything; falsy = None/0/empty; use `is None`

quiz.q: What makes a Python block end?
opts: The line is no longer indented
A semicolon at the end of the line
quiz.why: Indentation is syntax in Python — dedenting closes the block. No braces, no end keyword.

quiz.q: Which values are falsy in Python?
opts: Nothing is falsy — Python is strictly typed
quiz.why: None, 0, "", [], {}, and False are all falsy — so `if items:` is the idiomatic emptiness check.
== asks 'equal values?'; `is` asks 'same object in memory?' — that's why None is checked with `is None`.

code.title: Syntax basics in 20 lines
code.body:
# Dynamic typing — name tags, not declarations
price = 19.99
label = "pro"
price = label          # legal! the tag moves to a string

# Indentation is the block
if price == "pro":
    print("Pro plan")
    print("  unlimited reels")
print("always runs")   # dedented → outside the if

# f-strings: interpolation + formatting
rows = 1_234_567
print(f"Imported {rows:,} rows in {0.847:.2f}s")

# Truthiness
items = []
if not items:          # same as: if len(items) == 0
    print("empty list is falsy")

if price is None:
    pass               # explicit None check with `is`

# in + range
for i in range(3):     # 0, 1, 2
    if "pro" in label:
        print(f"  step {i + 1} of 3")
annot: 1_234_567 — underscores in numeric literals are legal and ignored (readability)
f-strings take ANY expression: f"{len(x) * 2} slots" is fine
range(3) is lazy — cheap even for range(10_000_000)

notes:
# Syntax Basics

## Dynamic typing
- `x = 5` — no type declaration. Variables are **names bound to objects**.
- Rebinding to another type is legal; errors appear at **runtime** (type hints + mypy fix this — Reel PY-08).

## Indentation & blocks
- Whitespace is syntax: indent = enter block, dedent = exit block.
- **4 spaces** per level (PEP 8); set the editor to convert tabs.
- Everything in a block must be indented — even single statements.

## f-strings
```python
f"Total: {price:.2f}"      # format spec inside braces
f"{n:,}"                   # thousands separators
f"{name.upper()} ok"       # any expression
```

## None & truthiness
- `None` = absence of a value (like null). Check with `is None`.
| Falsy | Truthy |
| --- | --- |
| `None`, `False`, `0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `()` | everything else |

## Operators
- `==` value equality · `is` identity (same object) · `in` membership.
- `range(5)` → lazy sequence 0..4; `list(range(5))` materializes it.
- `for i in range(n):` replaces C-style index loops in most cases.
